scenarios.title: One quarter becomes the trend
scenarios.prompt: Sales rose sharply last quarter. The new annual forecast assumes the same growth will continue, although the wider history is more variable.
scenarios.question: What should the forecast use as its starting point?

options.text: The most exciting recent quarter because it contains the newest information.
A broader distribution of comparable periods, then an explicit adjustment for current conditions.
The target required by the annual plan.

scenarios.explanation: Recent evidence matters, but it should be compared with a broader base rate. The adjustment should explain why this quarter is more informative than the rest.
missingEvidence: Specific drivers of the recent change.
Evidence that those drivers will continue.
scenarios.evidenceNote: Availability may give the latest quarter extra weight. A genuine structural change can justify a large adjustment when supported by independent evidence.
scenarios.nextAction: Set the historical baseline and document each reason for moving away from it.

scenarios.title: The risks do not add up
scenarios.prompt: A team estimates a 25% chance that the project will be late. When asked separately, it gives 20% to supplier delay, 20% to testing delay and 15% to staffing delay, with overlap left undefined.
scenarios.question: What should the team do next?

options.text: Keep every number because separate estimates are always more accurate.
Define overlap and reconcile the component risks with the total probability using comparable project data.
Choose the highest component probability as the total risk.

scenarios.explanation: Decomposed risks can receive more probability than the undivided event. Reconciliation and a reference distribution make the forecast internally checkable.
missingEvidence: The frequency of each cause in comparable projects.
A rule for combining component estimates.
scenarios.evidenceNote: Subadditivity is a useful lens for inconsistent whole-versus-part estimates. The numbers may also reflect unclear definitions rather than a stable cognitive effect.
scenarios.nextAction: Create mutually clear risk definitions and reconcile the total before publishing the forecast.

scenarios.title: The forecast was “basically right”
scenarios.prompt: A forecast missed badly. After the outcome, the owner says the result was always possible and that the original forecast should be read more generously.
scenarios.question: What would make the review useful?

options.text: Compare the outcome with the frozen forecast, range and update rules written before the result.
Allow the owner to restate what they meant now that the result is known.
Judge only whether the final narrative sounds reasonable.

scenarios.explanation: A frozen record prevents the forecast from changing in memory. Predefined update criteria also show whether new evidence should have triggered a revision before the outcome.
missingEvidence: The original point estimate or range.
Evidence available before each review date.
scenarios.evidenceNote: Hindsight is a plausible review risk because the original forecast is being reinterpreted after the result. Ambiguous documentation can be a separate process problem.
scenarios.nextAction: Score the forecast against the original record, then improve the future recording standard.
